(p-91) Surat Muhammad (ﷺ), also called Surat al-Qital (The Chapter of Fighting). It is Madani, though it has been said to be Makki. Its verses number thirty-eight.

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah﴾. That is: they turned away from Islam and from following its path, from *ṣadda ṣudūdan*, or they prevented people from it, from *ṣaddahu ṣaddan*, like those who provided food on the Day of Badr. It has been said that they were twelve men from among the polytheists who used to bar people from Islam and order them to disbelieve. It has also been said that they were the People of the Book who disbelieved and barred whoever among them and others wished to enter Islam. It has also been said that it is general, applying to everyone who disbelieves and bars.

﴿He has caused their deeds to go astray﴾. That is: He nullified them, made them void, and rendered them lost, with no effect whatsoever. However, this does not mean that He nullified and voided them after they had been otherwise. Rather, it means that He judged them to be null and lost. For the righteous deeds they did, such as maintaining the ties of kinship (*ṣilat al-arḥām*), hospitality to guests (*qirā al-aḍyāf*), freeing captives (*fakk al-usārā*), and other noble acts, have no effect from their origin, because they were not accompanied by faith. Or it means that He nullified what they did of scheming against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and barring from his way, by granting victory to His Messenger and making His religion manifest over all religions. This is the more fitting reading in light of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿So destruction for them, and He will make their deeds go astray﴾ and His saying ﴿When you meet...﴾ etc.

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. It is said: they are some people of Quraysh. It is said: they are from the Ansar. It is said: they are the believers among the People of the Book. It is said: it is general, applying to all.

﴿And believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾. The belief in that was singled out for mention, although it is included in what precedes it, to honour its status and to draw attention to the lofty position it holds among all the things that must be believed in, and because it is the root of all of them. For this reason it was emphasized by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾, by way of restricting truth to it. It is also said: its truthfulness lies in its being an abrogating (nasikh) revelation that is not itself abrogated (mansukh). Thus, according to this view, "al-haqq" (the truth) stands in contrast to what is transient (al-zail), while according to the first view it stands in contrast to falsehood (al-batil). In either case, His words ﴿from their Lord﴾ are a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring to the pronoun in "al-haqq". It is also read as "nazzala" in the active form (with the doubled letter, meaning "He sent down" gradually), as "anzala" in both forms (the active and the passive), and as "nazala" with the letter lightened.

﴿He will remove from them their misdeeds﴾, that is, He will cover them over through faith and righteous deeds.

﴿And He will set right their condition﴾, that is, their state in religion and in worldly life, through support and success.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ refers to what has been mentioned before: the misguiding of their deeds, the expiation of their evil deeds, and the setting right of their condition. It is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence) (p-92) whose *khabar* (predicate) is the statement of God, Exalted: ﴿because those who disbelieved followed falsehood, and because those who believed followed the truth from their Lord﴾. That is: this comes about because of the fact that the first group followed Satan (al-Shaytan), as Mujahid said, so they committed what they committed of disbelief and obstruction. Thus the explanation that following him is the cause of the misguidance mentioned also includes the explanation that the two (disbelief and obstruction) are its causes, since he is, definitely, a root that the two follow. And because the others followed the truth, which cannot be deviated from, coming from their Lord, so they did what they did of belief in it, in His Book, and of righteous deeds. Thus the explanation that following it is the cause of what was mentioned of expiation and setting right, after the implication that belief and righteous deeds are its causes, includes the explanation that these two are its causes, since it is the origin and source of them, inevitably. So there is no contradiction between the implication and the explicit statement in either of the two places. It is also permissible to understand *al-batil* (falsehood) as what is opposite to the truth, namely that which is perishing, departing, and has no basis at all. Then the explicit statement that following it is the cause of the misguiding and nullifying of their deeds is to explain that their nullification is due to the invalidity and passing away of its foundation. As for interpreting it as that which yields no benefit, this is not as it should be, because disbelief and obstruction are more heinous than that. So there is no justification for explicitly stating its causality for the misguiding of their deeds mentioned, by way of restriction (*qasr*), after the implication of their causality for it. So reflect on this. It is also permissible that by *al-batil* is meant the very disbelief and obstruction, and by *al-haqq* (truth) the very belief and righteous deeds. Then the specification of their causality for what was mentioned, of misguidance and of expiation and setting right, is an explicit statement of causality that was implied in both places.

﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ means: like that manner of wondrous coining.

﴿يَضْرِبُ اللَّهُ﴾ means: God clarifies.

﴿لِلنّاسِ أمْثالَهُمْ﴾ means: the conditions of the two groups and their attributes, which, in their strangeness, take the place of proverbs: namely, the first group's following of falsehood and their frustration and loss, and the others' following of the truth and their success and prosperity.

The Fa' in His words ﴿So when you encounter those who disbelieve﴾ indicates that the command in what follows it is ordered upon what precedes it. The misguidance of the disbelievers' deeds and their failure, and the righteousness of the believers' states and their success, necessitate that a fitting ruling be imposed on each of the two sides. That is, "So when the matter is as mentioned, then when you encounter them in battle."

﴿So strike the necks﴾. Its original form is: "Strike the necks with a striking." The verb was deleted, the verbal noun was placed first, and it was substituted for the verb and made to be annexed to the object. In this there is brevity and emphatic strengthening. Using it to refer to killing is a depiction of it in its most hideous form and a magnification of its gravity, and it guides the fighters to the easiest way of doing it.

﴿Until when you have subdued them﴾. That is: you have killed them in great numbers and made the killing severe, from "al-shay' al-thakhin," which is the thick, coarse thing. Or: you have weighed them down with killing and wounds until you have removed their ability to rise.

﴿Then bind the bonds﴾. Then take them captive and keep them secure. The wathaq (bond) is the name for that with which one is bound, and likewise al-withaq with a kasra, and it has been read with that.

﴿Then either grace after or ransom﴾. That is: either you bestow grace after that, or you accept ransom. The meaning is an option between killing, enslavement, grace and ransom. This is established according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, but according to us it is mansukh (abrogated). They said: this was revealed on the day of Badr and then abrogated, and the ruling is either killing or enslavement. From Mujahid: "There is today neither grace nor ransom; it is only Islam or the striking of the neck." It has been read as fida' like 'asa.

﴿Until the war lays down its burdens﴾. The burdens of war are its implements and its loads, which are the weapons and the horses and livestock that cannot be dispensed with. The laying down has been attributed to the war, while it belongs to its people, as a metaphorical attribution. "Until" is a limit according to al-Shafi'i, for one of the four matters or for them collectively. The meaning is: they will continue upon that forever until there is no war with the polytheists, in that they no longer have any strength. It was said: by 'Isa, peace be upon him, descending. As for Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him: if "the war" is taken to mean the war of Badr, then it is a limit for grace and ransom, and the meaning is: they are granted grace and ransomed until the war of Badr lays down its burdens. If it is taken to mean the genus, then it is a limit for the striking and binding, and the meaning is: they are killed and taken captive until the genus of war lays down its burdens, in that no strength remains for the polytheists. It was said: its burdens are its sins, that is: until the polytheists abandon their polytheism and their sins by accepting Islam.

﴿That﴾. That is: the matter is that, or they did that.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾. He would have punished them with some causes of destruction and annihilation.

﴿But﴾. He did not will that.

﴿That He may test some of you by means of others﴾. So He commanded you to fight and tested you with the disbelievers, so that you might strive against them and thereby merit the great reward according to the necessity of the promise; and tested the disbelievers by you, so that He might treat them at your hands with some of His punishment, so that some of them might be deterred from disbelief.

﴿And those who are killed in the way of Allah﴾. That is: those who were martyred. It has been read qatalu (they fought), that is: they strove, and qatalu (they killed), and qutilu (they were killed).

﴿He will not waste their deeds﴾. That is: He will not lose them. It has been read yudalla a'malu-hum in the passive, and yudilla a'malahum from dalla (to go astray). From Qatadah: it was revealed concerning the day of Uhud.
﴿He will guide them﴾ in this world to the most right course of affairs, and in the Hereafter to the reward; or, He will make their guidance firm. ﴿And will set right their state﴾.

﴿And He will admit them into Paradise, which He has made known to them﴾. This is said to mean: in the world, by mentioning its attributes, such that they longed for it; or, He made it clear to them, such that each person knows his abode and is guided to it as though he had been its inhabitant since it was created. And it is narrated from Muqatil that the angel assigned to his deeds in the world walks before him, and makes known to him everything that Allah the Exalted has given him. Or (He made it "fragrant," *tayyabahā*, for them, from *al-'arf*, which is good scent). Or He delimited it for them and set it apart from the rest of the abode (*'arf al-dar*), so each one's Paradise is defined and distinct. The clause is either a fresh sentence (*mustaʾnafa*) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with *qad* implied or not implied.

O you who have believed, if you support Allah [i.e., His religion and His Messenger],

He will support you [against your enemies] and make you firm in your positions [in the places and stations of battle, or upon the path of Islam].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 8:

﴿And those who disbelieve – then ruin (ta'san) for them﴾. Ta's (ruin) means destruction, stumbling, falling, evil, distance, and abasement. A man is called ta'is and ta'is. Its being in the accusative (intisabuhu) is by its verb, which is obligatorily omitted according to what is heard (sama'an), i.e., "so he said: ta'san for them," or "so He decreed: ta'san for them." His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and He misguided their deeds﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon it, being included with it within the scope of the informative nature (khabariyyah) of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul).

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 47, verse 9:

﴿That﴾ i.e., what was mentioned of misfortune (al-ta'is) and the nullification of their deeds.

﴿Because﴾ on account of the fact that ﴿they disliked what Allah has sent down﴾ of the Qur'an, (p-94) because of what it contains of tawhid and the rest of the rulings, which oppose what they were accustomed to and what their commanding selves (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su') desired.

﴿So He nullified﴾ on account of that.

﴿their deeds﴾ which, had they performed them together with faith, they would have been rewarded for.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 10:

﴿Have they not travelled in the earth?﴾ That is: they sat in their places and did not travel in it.

﴿So that they might look at how was the end of those before them﴾ of the destroying nations, for indeed the traces of their dwellings inform about their histories. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God destroyed upon them﴾ is a resumptive (istinaf) clause built upon a question arising from the speech, as if it were said: "How was their end?" So it was said: God, exalted is He, uprooted upon them what pertained to them of their own selves, their families and their wealth. It is said: "dammarahu" means he destroyed him; and "dammara 'alayhi" means he destroyed upon him what pertains to him.

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾ That is: and for these disbelievers who follow their course.

﴿Their like﴾ the like of their ends or their punishments, but not in the sense that these have like what those had, and multiples of it; rather, it is its like. It was put in the plural in view of its being like the multiple ends according to the multiplicity of the nations punished. It was said: it is possible that their punishment is more severe than the punishment of the earlier ones, since they were killed and taken captive by the hands of those whom they used to mock and belittle, and being killed by the hand of the like is more painful than destruction by a general calamity. It was also said: the intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is the earlier ones, by way of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, as if it were said: "God destroyed upon them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter are their like."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 11:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the establishment of the like of the punishments of the earlier nations for these people.

﴿Because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe﴾, that is, their Helper against their enemies. It is also read as "waliyy alladhina" (the Friend of those who believe).

﴿And because the disbelievers have no protector (mawla)﴾, so that none can ward off from them the retribution and punishment that has befallen them. This does not contradict His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Mawla (Protector)﴾, for the word mawla there means "owner" (malik).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ — an explanation of the ruling of His (exalted be He) guardianship (wilayah) over them and its fruit in the Hereafter.

﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves﴾ — that is, they benefit in this world from its enjoyments (mata').

﴿And eat as the cattle eat﴾ — heedless of their consequences.

﴿And the Fire is their abode﴾ — that is, a place of lodging and staying. The clause is either a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the waw of "yakulun" (they eat), or a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf).

**﴿And how many⟩** — (وَكَأيِّنْ) is a compound word made of the particle ﴿ك﴾ (kaf) and ﴿أيٍّ﴾ (ayy), meaning "how many" in the sense of an informative (khabariyyah) quantifier. Its position (mahall) is in the nominative case, as the subject of an inceptive (mubtada'). The phrase ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ ("from a town") is a specifier (tamyiz) for it. The words ﴿هِيَ أشَدُّ قُوَّةً مِن قَرْيَتِكَ﴾ ("it was stronger in power than your town") are an attribute (sifah) of ﴿قَرْيَةٍ﴾, just as ﴿الَّتِي أخْرَجَتْكَ﴾ ("which expelled you") is an attribute of ﴿قَرْيَتِكَ﴾. In both cases the governing noun (al-mudaf) has been omitted and its rulings have been applied to the words that follow, as is made clear by the predicate (khabar), which is the verse ﴿أهْلَكْناهُمْ﴾ ("We destroyed them"). The meaning is: "And how many a population of a town were stronger than the people of your town, who were the cause of your departure from among them." The description of the first town as having greater strength serves to indicate that the second town is more deserving of destruction because of the weakness of its strength; likewise, the description of the second town by the expulsion of him (upon him be peace) serves to indicate that it is more deserving of destruction because of the gravity of its crime.

In this same manner is the saying of al-Nabighah:

Kulayb, by my life, was more helpful as a supporter, and less guilty of offence, than you, who was drenched with blood.

The verse ﴿فَلا ناصِرَ لَهُمْ﴾ ("so there is no helper for them") is an explanation that they cannot be rescued from the punishment through the aid of helpers and supporters, following the explanation that they cannot be rescued from it by themselves. The particle ﴿الفاء﴾ (fa') is for the sequencing of the mention of what is by others after the mention of what is by oneself. This is a narration of a past situation (hikayat hal madiyah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 14:

﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾ is an affirmation of the contrast between the two states of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, and of the fact that the former are in the highest of the ʿIlliyyin (ʿIlliyyūn, the highest levels of Paradise) while the latter are in the lowest of the lowest (asfal sāfilīn). It also explains the reason for the state each of them has. The hamza (alif-hamza, interrogative particle) is for denial (inkār), and the fa' (fāʾ) is for conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon an implied clause (muqaddar) that the context requires. It has been read without it (i.e., without the fa'). And "man" (man, "one who") is an expression for the believers who hold firmly to the proofs of the religion. Making it an expression for the Prophet (ﷺ), or for him together with the believers, is not supported by the noble arrangement of the verse, since placing him (ﷺ) in comparison with them is something his lofty station (manṣib, rank) rejects. The implied sense is: Is the matter not as has been mentioned? So one who is steadfast upon a manifest proof and a luminous demonstration from the Lord of his affair, who cherishes and nurtures him, namely the Noble Qur'an and the rest of the miracles and rational proofs.

﴿Like one whose evil deeds have been made attractive to him﴾, [namely] of shirk and the rest of the sins, while being in himself the worst of ugly things.

﴿And they follow﴾ as a result of that embellishment.

﴿Their desires﴾, the deviating ones, and they immerse themselves in the various kinds of misguidance, without there being for them any doubt that makes them imagine the soundness of what they have adopted, let alone any proof that indicates it. The plural of the last two pronouns is by consideration of the meaning of "man," just as the singular of the first two is by consideration of its wording.

﴿The likeness of the Garden promised to the God-conscious﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf), brought to explain the excellences of the Garden promised to the believers just mentioned, and to describe the manner of its rivers, whose flowing beneath it was indicated. They are described as "the God-conscious" (al-muttaqūn, those mindful of God) to signal that faith and righteous deeds fall under taqwā (God-consciousness), which means performing all the obligations and abstaining from all the misdeeds. Its "likeness" (mathal) is its wondrous description. It is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted. Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl estimated it as: "the likeness of the Garden is what you hear." And God's words ﴿in it are rivers﴾ and so on explain it. Sībawayh estimated it as: "what is recited to you is the likeness of the Garden." The first is more suitable to the opening of this noble composition. It was also said: "mathal" is superfluous, like the addition of the noun in the words of one who said: [Until the year's end, then the name of peace be upon you both]. In that case "the Garden" is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿in it are rivers﴾ and so on.

﴿of water unchanging﴾: not altered in taste or smell. It was also read as "ghayri ʾasin" (a variant recitation).

﴿and rivers of milk whose taste never changes﴾: by becoming sharp or sour, as the milks of this world do.

﴿and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾: delicious, with no unpleasantness of taste or smell, no harm of intoxication, and no hangover; it is pure pleasure. "Ladhdhah" is either a feminine form of ladhdh, meaning delicious, or a verbal noun used as an adjective for emphasis. It was read "ladhdhatun" in the nominative, as an attribute of "rivers," and in the accusative as a reason, meaning: for the sake of the drinkers' pleasure.

﴿and rivers of honey, clarified﴾: not mixed with wax, the dregs of bees, or anything else. In this there is a representation of what in the Garden serves as drinks, in kinds that are pleasant and enjoyable in this world, by freeing them from whatever spoils or diminishes them, and adorning them with what makes them abundant and lasting.

﴿And for them therein﴾ alongside what has been mentioned of the varieties of rivers.

﴿of every fruit﴾: that is, a kind of every fruit.

﴿and forgiveness﴾: that is, for them is a great forgiveness, whose extent cannot be measured. God's words ﴿from their Lord﴾ relate to an omitted element which is an attribute of "forgiveness," confirming what the indefiniteness conveys of intrinsic grandeur with the grandeur of attribution. That is: it proceeds from their Lord.

God's words ﴿Is it like one who abides in the Fire?﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "Is one who abides in this Garden, as was promised, like one who abides in the Fire," as God's words ﴿and the Fire is their abode﴾ express. It was also said: it is the predicate of "the likeness of the Garden," with an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "Is the likeness of the Garden like the likeness of the recompense of one who abides in the Fire?" or "Is the likeness of the people of the Garden like the likeness of one who abides in the Fire?" The interrogative particle of denial is dropped, and what was dropped was omitted, depicting the obstinacy of one who equates between the one who holds to the clear proof and the one who follows his desires, by the obstinacy of one who equates the Garden, described by the sublime attributes detailed, with the Fire.

﴿And they will be given boiling water to drink﴾ in place of those drinks.

﴿so that it cuts their intestines﴾ because of its extreme heat. It was said: when it approaches them, it scorches their faces, and the skin of their heads peels off; then when they drink it, it cuts their intestines.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 16:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ — they are the hypocrites. The singular pronoun is used in view of the wording of "man" (مَن), just as the plural is used later in view of its meaning. They used to attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and hear his speech, but they would not retain it, nor would they observe it with the observance it deserved, out of their own negligence.

﴿Until, when they go out from your presence, they say to those who were given knowledge﴾ — from among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿"What did he just say?"﴾ — that is, what was it that he said just now, in the manner of mockery, though it takes the form of a question. "Ānifan" (آنِفًا) derives from their saying "anafa al-shay'" (أنَفَ الشَّيْءُ), meaning "what has preceded from it." It is a metaphor taken from the bodily organ (the nose, "anf"), and from it come "istan'afa al-shay'" (اسْتَأْنَفَ الشَّيْءَ) and "i'tanafa" (ائْتَنَفَ). It is an adverb of time, meaning "a time that has just begun," or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "qāla" (قالَ). It has also been read as "anfan" (أنْفًا).

﴿Those are the ones﴾ — those described by what has been mentioned.

﴿Whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾ — because they had no inclination toward good at all.

﴿And who follow their own desires﴾ — the false ones; therefore they did what they did, of which there is no good.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 17:

﴿And those who are guided﴾ to the path of truth.

﴿He increases them﴾, i.e., Allah the Exalted.

﴿in guidance﴾ through enabling success (tawfiq) and inspiration (ilham).

﴿And gives them their piety﴾: He helps them to their piety, or gives them its reward, or makes clear to them what they should guard against.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 18:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but the Hour?﴾ That is, the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that it come upon them suddenly﴾ means: it will surprise them with a sudden arrival, and suddenness is the surprise, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the Hour" (al-sa'ah). The meaning is: they are not reminded by the mention of the terrors of the former nations, nor by the report of the coming of the Hour and the great terrors it contains, and they are waiting for nothing that would lead to remembrance except the coming of the Hour itself, suddenly. It has been read as "baghatan" with a fatha on the ghayn. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for its portents have already come﴾ is a causal clause explaining its surprising arrival, not its coming in general, in the sense that there remains none of the matters that necessitate remembrance awaited by them, other than the coming of the Hour itself, since its portents have already come; yet they did not pay heed to it and did not count it among the beginnings of its arrival, so its coming will certainly be by way of surprise. Ashrat (portents) is the plural of sharth (sign), with the vowel on the shin and the ra' as in "sharat", and it means a sign. What is meant by them is his being sent (ﷺ), the splitting of the moon, and similar things. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How then for them is their remembrance when it comes to them?﴾ is a judgment on their error and the corruption of their opinion in delaying remembrance until its arrival, by explaining the impossibility of the benefit of remembrance at that time, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ That is: and how will they have their remembrance when it comes to them? This is on the reading that "anna" is a predicate preceding its subject, "dhikrahum" is the subject, and "idha ja'athum" is a parenthetical clause placed between them, as a symbol of the extreme speed of its arrival. The word "coming" is unrestricted from the condition of suddenness, because the basis of the impossibility of the benefit of remembrance is that it occurs at its coming, absolutely, not restricted by the condition of suddenness. It has been read as "in ta'tihim" (if it comes upon them), on the basis that it is a new conditional clause whose apodosis is ﴿then how for them﴾ etc. The meaning is: if the Hour comes upon them suddenly, since its signs have already appeared, then how will they be reminded and admonished when it comes to them?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 19:

﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾. That is: when you have known that the axis of happiness is monotheism (tawhid) and obedience, and the basis of wretchedness is associating partners with Allah (shirk) and disobedience, then remain steadfast in what you are upon of knowledge of the Oneness and acting in accordance with it.

﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin﴾. This is what may occasionally proceed from him, upon him be prayers and peace, of leaving what is better (tark al-awla). It is expressed as a "sin" in view of his exalted station. How could it not be so? For the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near (to Allah). It is also a guidance for him, upon him be prayers and peace, toward humility, self-abasement, and regarding one's deeds as insufficient.

﴿And for the believing men and the believing women﴾. That is: for their sins, by supplicating for them and encouraging them toward what calls for their forgiveness. Repeating the particle of seeking forgiveness (istighfar) indicates the difference in the genus of its two objects. And omitting the annexed noun (mudaf) and placing the annexed-to noun (mudaf ilayh) in its place indicates their deep-rootedness in sin and their extreme need for seeking forgiveness.

﴿And Allah knows your movement﴾ in this world, for it is stages that must inevitably be traversed. ﴿And your dwelling place﴾ in the hereafter, for it is the abodes of your residence. So He does not command you except what is good for you in both; so hasten to comply with what He has commanded you, for that is what matters most to you in both states. It has also been said: He knows all your conditions, so nothing of them is hidden from Him.

(p-98)

﴿And those who believe say: "Why has a surah not been sent down?"﴾ out of their eagerness for jihad.

﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾ That is: "Would that a surah had been sent down in which jihad is commanded."

﴿But when a decisive surah is sent down, in which fighting is mentioned﴾ by way of command to it, that is: a surah that is clear, with no ambiguity and no possibility of any meaning other than the obligation of fighting. From Qatadah: every surah in which fighting is mentioned is muhkamah (decisive), not abrogated. It is also read as "fa-idha nuzzilat surah" (p-98), and it is read as "wa-dhakara" with the verb attributed to God's pronoun, and "al-qital" in the accusative.

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ That is: weakness in religion. It is also said: hypocrisy, which is the more evident and better suited to the context of this noble composition.

﴿looking at you with the look of one fainting from death.﴾ That is: their eyes stare out of cowardice and panic, like the state of one overcome by the swoon of death.

﴿So woe to them.﴾ That is: woe to them. It is the elative form from al-wali, meaning nearness. It is also said that it derives from "ala", meaning a curse upon them, that what is hateful befall them, or that their affair return to that. It is also said that it is derived from "al-wayl" (woe), and its original form is "awyal", the ayn being moved to after the lam, so its pattern is "afla'".

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 21:

﴿Obedience and honorable speech.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), meaning: "Their affair is obedience... etc." Or: "Obedience and honorable speech is better for them." Or it is a quotation of their words, and this is supported by the reading of Ubayy (ibn Kaʿb): "They say: obedience and honorable speech," meaning: "Our affair is that."

﴿Then when the matter is resolved upon﴾ The resolve (ʿazm), which is earnestness (jidd), is attributed to the matter (al-amr), while it belongs to its people; this is a metaphor (majaz), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, that is of the steadfast resolutions of affairs﴾. The governing element of the time expression (ʿamil al-zarf) is omitted, meaning: they opposed and held back. It was said: they broke their word. It was said: they disliked it. It was said: it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then if they had been true to Allah﴾, following the manner of your saying: "If food came to me, then if you had come to me, I would have fed you," meaning: then if they had been true to Him, exalted is He, in what they said of words expressing eagerness for jihad, by acting in accordance with its requirement.

﴿It would have been﴾, that is: the truthfulness.

﴿better for them﴾. In this is an indication that all of them share in what is related of them in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾. It was said: "then if they had been true to Him in faith, and their hearts had agreed with their tongues in that." And whichever of these it is, the intended ones are those in whose hearts is a disease, and they are the ones addressed by His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 22:

﴿Then, if you were to turn away﴾ ... etc. It is by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), to emphasize the rebuke and intensify the reproach, i.e., is it to be expected of you?

﴿If you were to take charge﴾ of the affairs of the people and rule over them.

﴿That you would cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship﴾ by vying with one another for dominion and being greedy for worldly life. For whoever observes your conditions, which indicate weakness in religion and eagerness for this world, at a time when you have been commanded to wage jihad, which is an expression for securing every good and righteousness and repelling every evil and corruption, while you are commanded to obedience and to speaking what is good, would expect from you, once your reins are loosed and you become rulers, what was mentioned of corruption and severing of kinship. It has been said: "If you turn away from Islam," that you would return to what you were upon in the Jahiliyyah of corruption on earth through mutual haughtiness and plundering, and severing of kinship by some relatives fighting others and burying daughters alive. In this there is a point: whatever falls within the scope of a conditional in such a context must have its objectionable character considered in terms of the corruptions it entails, not in terms of its own essence. And there is no doubt that turning away from Islam is the head of every evil and corruption, so it is fitting that it be made the principal element of the rebuke, not merely a means of rebuking by what is lesser than it of corruptions.

It was read as "wulliytum" (passive), meaning: you were made rulers. It was also read as "tawallaytum," meaning: rulers of tyranny took you as their allies, and you went out with them and assisted them in corruption and severing of kinship. It was read as "wa-taqaṭṭa'ū" from taqaṭṭu'  (with one of the two tā' elided), and then the accusative of "arḥāmakum" is by removal of the preposition, i.e., "in your kinship ties." It was read as "wa-taqṭa'ū" from qaṭ' (cutting off). And attaching the pronoun to "ʿasā" is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, whereas the Banū Tamīm say: ʿasā an tafʿala and ʿasā an tafʿalū.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 23:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the addressees, shifted to by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person, here from direct address to third-person reference), signifying that mentioning their failings necessitated removing them from the rank of direct address and reporting their dreadful conditions to others. It is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿those whom Allah has cursed﴾, i.e., He has removed them far from His mercy.

﴿and has made them deaf﴾ to hearing the truth, because they made themselves deaf to it through their bad choice.

﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ because they turned a blind eye to the signs that they witness, those placed in the souls and on the horizons.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 24:

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ That is: will they not observe it, nor peruse it, nor the admonitions and deterrents it contains, so that they would not fall into the destructive sins into which they have fallen?

﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ So that no remembrance (dhikr) reaches them at all. "Am" (ام, "or") is disjunctive (munqati'a), and what it implies is the meaning of "bal" (بل, "rather"), shifting from the rebuke for not reflecting to the rebuke for their hearts being locked, not accepting reflection and contemplation. The hamza (ء, interrogative particle) is for affirmation (taqrir). The indefiniteness of "hearts" (qulub) is either to magnify their condition and make grave their state, by implying that their matter in hardness and ignorance is such that it is as if it were said: upon hearts that are unfamiliar, whose condition is not known and whose degree of hardness cannot be measured; or because what is meant by them is the hearts of some of them, namely the hypocrites (munafiqun). The attribution of the locks to them (idafa) indicates that these are locks specific to them, suited to them, not of the same kind as the other known locks. It is also read "aqfaluha" and "iqfaluha," the latter as a verbal noun (masdar).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾ i.e., they returned to what they had been upon of disbelief (kufr). They are the hypocrites (munafiqun) who were described in what preceded with sickness of the hearts and other ugly acts and states, for they had disbelieved in him (ﷺ).

﴿after guidance had become clear to them﴾ through the manifest proofs and the overpowering miracles. It is said: they are the Jews. And it is said: the People of the Two Books (Ahl al-Kitab) altogether disbelieved in him (ﷺ) after they found his description in their Books and knew that he was the one described by it. His saying, Most High: ﴿Satan has beguiled them﴾ is a sentence of subject and predicate that occurs as the predicate of inna. That is, he made easy for them the mounting of great matters, from taswil (beguilement), which is slackening (al-istirkha'). It is said: it is from al-sawl, the lightened form of al-su'al (request), due to the persistence of the heart; so the meaning of sawwala lahu amran then is that he caused him to fall into his wish, for al-su'l is the wish (al-umniyya). And it was read as "suwwila" in the passive voice, with the omission of the modified noun, i.e., "the plot of Satan."

﴿and I shall give them respite﴾ He promised them in hopes and aspirations. It is said: God Most High granted them respite and did not hasten punishment upon them. And it was read as "wa-amla late lahum" in the first-person speaker form, so the meaning is: Satan misleads them and I give them respite. They said: it is for the state (lil-hal) or for the resumption (lil-istinaf). And it was read as "umli lahum" in the passive voice, i.e., they were given respite and their lifespan was extended.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned of their apostasy, not to the respite (al-imla', divine postponement), as is reported from al-Wahidi, nor to the embellishment (al-taswil, the making of an action seem fair), as has been said, because neither of these is the consequence of the statement that follows. The word ﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the phrase of the Exalted ﴿because they﴾, meaning: because of the fact that they.

﴿said﴾: that is, the hypocrites just mentioned, not the Jews who disbelieved in him (ﷺ) after they found his description in the Torah (al-Tawrah), as has been said. For their disbelief in him is not because of this statement, even if it were assumed that it was uttered by them, whether those addressed by it were the hypocrites or the polytheists according to the view of the one who holds this. Rather, [their disbelief began] from the time of his mission (ﷺ).

﴿to those who hated what God had sent down﴾: that is, to the Jews who hated the descent of the Qur'an upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), although they knew that it was from God the Exalted, out of envy and out of desire for its descent upon them themselves. It is not addressed to the polytheists, as has been said. For the words of the Exalted ﴿We will obey you in some of the matter﴾ are certainly an expression of what is related of them by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book: "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely help you"?﴾ They were the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir, whom they used to befriend and show affection to. By "some of the matter" concerning which they indicated non-obedience to them, they intended to make apparent their disbelief and to declare their affair openly by action before fighting them and expelling them from their homes. For they used to refuse that, before the pressing necessity that calls for it touched them, because of the worldly benefits they had in displaying faith. They were only saying to them what they said in secret, as the words of the Exalted indicate: ﴿And God knows their secrets﴾, that is, their concealment of what they said to the Jews. It has been recited as "their secrets" (asrarahum), that is, all their secrets, of which this statement of theirs is one. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid) that confirms what precedes it and includes the exposure in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So how will it be when the angels take them in death﴾, is for the sequencing (tartib) of what follows it upon what precedes it. "Kayfa" (how) is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb which is the operator of the temporal adverbs (al-zuruf), as if it were said: they do in their lives what they do of deceits, so how will they do when the angels take them in death? It has also been said that it is in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "So how is their state, or their deceits, when the angels take them...", etc.

It is also read "tawaffahum" (تَوَفَّاهُمْ), in which case it is either a past tense verb or a present tense verb with one of its two taa's elided.

﴿Striking their faces and their backs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the subject of "tawaffathum" or from its object, and it is a depiction of their being taken in death upon the most dreadful and severe of states, regarding the faces and backs. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that no one dies while in disobedience except that the angels strike his face and his back.

That (is) the dreadful death [of the angels].

Because they followed what angered Allah, [namely] disbelief and sins,

and they disliked His pleasure, i.e., what He is pleased with of faith and obedience, in that they disbelieved after having believed, and departed from obedience by what they did in dealing with the Jews.

So He made void their deeds, for this reason,

[namely] the deeds they performed while in faith, of acts of obedience, or after that, of acts of righteousness which, had they performed them while in faith, they would have benefited from.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 29:

﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are the hypocrites, whose shameful conditions have been detailed; they are described by their earlier attribute, because it is the basis for what is censured of them in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿that Allah will never bring forth their malice﴾. So "am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and "an" is the light form of "anna" (that), whose subject, the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), is omitted, and "lan" (never) with what is in its scope is its predicate. And al-adghan (malice) is the plural of ghidn, which is hiqd (rancor), meaning: "Rather, do those in whose hearts is rancor and enmity toward the believers suppose that Allah will never bring forth their rancor (ahqad) (p-101) and will never expose it to His Messenger (ﷺ) and to the believers, so that their affairs remain concealed?" The meaning is that this is something that hardly falls within the realm of possibility.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 30:

﴿And if We willed﴾ to show them (to you).

﴿We would surely have shown them to you﴾, i.e., We would have made you recognize them by signs that let you know them by their very persons, a recognition bordering on sight. The shift to the first-person plural "Nun of Majesty" (nun al-'azamah) serves to highlight the care taken in the showing.

﴿So you would surely have recognized them by their mark﴾, by their sign with which We brand them. It was narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Nothing of the hypocrites remained hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after this verse. He used to recognize them by their mark. We were once on some of the campaigns, and among them were nine hypocrites whom the people complained about. They slept one night, and in the morning each one of them had written on him: 'This is a hypocrite.'" The lam is the lam of the answer (lam al-jawab), repeated in the conjoined clause for emphasis, and the fa' (fa) indicates that the recognition follows upon the showing. As for what is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tenor of their speech﴾, it is for an oath that is omitted, and "lahn al-qawl" (the tenor of speech) means its manner and style, or its inclination toward allusion and indirect meaning. From this comes the saying about one who errs: "laahin" (one who has deviated), because he has turned his speech away from the straight course of correctness.

﴿And Allah knows your deeds﴾, so He will recompense you according to your intention. This is a promise to the believers and an announcement that their state is contrary to the state of the hypocrites.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 31:

﴿And We will surely test you﴾ by the command to fight (jihad) and similar burdensome obligations.

﴿Until We know those among you who strive (mujahidin) and the patient (al-sabirin)﴾ under the hardships of jihad, with knowledge that comes into being through actual occurrence (ilm fi'li), upon which reward is based.

﴿And We will test your reports (akhbar)﴾, meaning what is reported about your deeds, so that their good and bad become manifest. It is read as "wa-yabluwa" with the ya' (yabluwa), and it is read as "nabluwa" with the waw silent, upon the reading "wa-nahnu nabluwa" (and We test).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 32:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar⁠﴾ [people] ﴿from the way of Allah and oppose the Messenger⁠﴾ and act hostilely toward him.

﴿after guidance has become clear to them⁠﴾ through what they witnessed of his description (ﷺ) in the Torah, and through the miracles that appeared at his hands and the signs that were sent down upon him. They were the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir, or those who fed [the polytheists] on the day of Badr.

﴿will not harm Allah⁠﴾ by their disbelief and their obstruction

﴿in the least⁠﴾ of anything, or [will not harm] the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in any way by their opposition. The object has been omitted to magnify him and to express the enormity of their opposition.

﴿And He will render their deeds void⁠﴾, i.e., their schemes which they set up to nullify His religion, and to oppose His Messenger (ﷺ). Thus they will not reach through them what they sought of mischief, and they will bring them nothing but killing and exile from their homelands.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 33:

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds.﴾ [Nullify your deeds] by that by which these people nullified their deeds: disbelief (kufr), hypocrisy (nifaq), self-admiration (ujb), showing off (riya'), reminding of favors (mann) and harm (adha), and the like. And there is no proof in it for the nullification (ihbat) of acts of obedience by major sins (kaba'ir).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 34:

(p-102) ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah, then die while they are disbelievers — Allah will never forgive them.﴾ This is a ruling that encompasses every person who dies in disbelief, even if its revelation is authentically related concerning the people of the well (al-qalib).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 35:**

﴿So do not weaken﴾, that is: do not become feeble.

﴿and call to peace﴾, that is: and do not call the disbelievers to reconciliation out of weakness, for that is giving them the lowest term. It is permissible that it be in the subjunctive, with *an* (أنْ) implied, as an answer to the prohibition. It has also been recited as "*wa-lā tadda'ū*" (وَلا تَدَّعُوا), from *idda'ā al-qawmu tada'aw* (ادَّعى القَوْمُ تَداعَوْا), like *ertamaw al-ṣayd* (ارْتَمَوُا الصَّيْدَ) and *tarāmaw-hu* (وتَرامَوْهُ), and from it *tarā'aw al-hilāl* (تَراءَوُا الهِلالَ). The form *tafā'ala* (صيغَةُ التَّفاعُلِ) may be used to express the act proceeding from several parties without regard to its falling upon one of them. From it is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾, on one of the two readings. The *fa'* (الفاءُ) indicates that the prohibition follows from what preceded it, namely the command to obey.

The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿while you are the superior ones﴾ is a circumstantial clause (جُمْلَةٌ حالِيَّةٌ) that confirms the meaning of the prohibition and emphasizes the obligation to desist. Likewise the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is with you﴾, for their being the superior ones and His, Mighty and Majestic, being their helper are among the strongest reasons to avoid what gives the impression of humiliation and servility. Likewise His, Exalted is He, fulfilling the rewards of deeds, as indicated by the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿and He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾, that is: He will not waste them. It is from *watartu al-rajul* (وَتَرْتَ الرَّجُلَ), meaning when you kill for a man a slain person from his child, brother or close kin, so that you isolate him from them, from *al-watr* (الوَتْر), which is the single (الفَرْد). The withholding of reward in return for deeds is expressed by *al-watr*, which is the waste of something of great worth, from lives and wealth. Yet deeds do not necessitate reward according to the principle of the People of the Sunnah (أهْلِ السُّنَّةِ), in order to display the utmost kindness by depicting the reward in the form of a due right, and by treating the withholding of reward as the waste and destruction of the greatest rights. This has already been mentioned in the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So their Lord answered them: I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, the life of this world is but play and amusement.﴾ It has no permanence, and no regard should be given to it.

﴿And if you believe and fear Allah, He will give you your rewards﴾, i.e., the reward of your faith and your god-consciousness (taqwa), from the enduring good deeds (al-baqiyat al-salihat) for which those who strive should compete.

﴿And He will not ask you for your wealth﴾ in such a way that its payment would harm your livelihood. Rather, He has limited the demand to a small portion of it, namely one-fortieth (rub' al-'ushr), which you pay to your poor.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 37:

﴿If He asks it of you﴾ i.e., your wealth.

﴿and He presses you (yuhfikum)﴾ i.e., He would exert you by demanding all of it, for al-ihfa' (pressing) and al-ilhaf (insistence) mean exaggeration and reaching the utmost limit. It is said: "ahfa sharibahu" (he cut his moustache down to the root) when he uprooted it entirely.

﴿and you become miserly (tabkhalu)﴾ so you do not give.

﴿and He would bring forth your rancors (adghanakum)﴾ i.e., your grudges. The pronoun in "yukhriju" (He brings forth) refers to God Most High, and the reading with the royal "we" (nun of majesty) supports this. Alternatively, it refers to miserliness, since it is the cause of rancors. It was also read as "yakhruju" (it comes forth), from al-khuruj (coming out), with the ya' and the ta', with "al-adghan" (the rancors) as its grammatical subject.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 47, verse 38:**

﴿Here you are, you who﴾ means: you, O you who are addressed.

(p-103) These are the ones described. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿are invited to spend in the way of Allah﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that confirms what precedes it), or a relative clause (sila) for "these," on the basis that it means "those who," i.e., "Here you are, you who are invited." In this there is a great rebuke and a belittling of their status. Spending in the way of Allah encompasses the expense of military campaigns (ghazw), zakat (obligatory alms), and other things.

﴿Among you there is one who is stingy﴾ means: some people are stingy. This is within the scope of the evidence for the preceding conditional statement.

﴿And whoever is stingy, is only stingy against himself﴾: the benefit of spending and the harm of stinginess both return to him. Stinginess (bukhl) is used with "'an" and "'ala," because it includes the meanings of withholding (imsak) and transgression (ta'addi).

﴿And Allah is the Rich﴾, without any other.

﴿And you are the poor﴾: so He commands you to what He commands because you need the benefits in it. If you comply, it is for your own good, and if you turn away, it is to your own detriment. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if you turn away﴾ is coordinated with ﴿And if you believe﴾, meaning: and if you turn away from faith and piety.

﴿He will replace you with another people﴾: He will install in your place another people.

﴿Then they will not be like you﴾ in turning away from faith and piety, but rather they will be eager for them both. It has been said: they are the Ansar. It has been said: they are the angels. It has been said: they are the people of Persia, for it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about "the people," and Sulayman was beside him, so he struck his thigh and said: "This one and his people. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if faith were suspended from the Pleiades, men from Persia would reach it." It has been said: the non-Arabs (ajam). It has been said: the Byzantines (Rum).

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Muhammad, it is a right upon Allah, mighty and majestic, that He give him to drink from the rivers of Paradise."
